weekly payments adding up to two or three times the price (1950s dollars)
years of payments on a contract house, lost with one late payment (1950s dollars)
a deposit kept for invented charges (1950s dollars)
a flat utility charge above real usage, for a year (1950s dollars)
fees added to one late rent (1950s dollars)
A house on the next street, and they're finally selling to us!
Bought cheap from panicked sellers, then marked up by half or more for you.
Sold on contract: you won't hold the deed until the very last payment.
The same speculator scared the sellers into selling and now sells to you. That's blockbusting.
a house marked up by half after panic selling (1950s dollars)
Fire insurance: our special policy for your area.
It costs far more than the same policy across the line, when they'll write one at all.
One claim and the policy is cancelled at renewal.
Insurers drew the same red lines the lenders did.
a year of an overpriced 'special' policy (1950s dollars)
A room in a converted house: cheap, and close to the plant.
Per square foot, the rent is higher than the big houses across town.
The rent climbs as more families are packed into the building.
An absentee owner splits big houses into many units; the more crowded, the more profit.
a year of rent above what bigger houses cost across town (1950s dollars)

Refuse, and eminent domain takes the house anyway, on their schedule.

a buyout below what any allowed house costs (1950s dollars)
A nice house across town. The realtor says you'd love it there.
The deed carries a covenant: no Black owners.
Since Shelley v. Kraemer (1948) courts can't enforce it, but the realtor won't tell you that.
Developers, realtors and lenders wrote those covenants in together.
a deposit lost on a house the covenant won't let you keep (1950s dollars)

a repair loan secured by the house, at a crushing rate (1950s dollars)

Your home is valued below what it would fetch across the line.
The low appraisal blocks the refinance you needed this year.

the value a low appraisal takes off your home (1950s dollars)

A guaranteed mortgage at a fair rate, with a small down payment.

A public benefit, earned in service.
a fair mortgage with a small down payment (1950s dollars)

Free to file, and steering is against the law since the Fair Housing Act (1968).

a home you're no longer steered away from (1950s dollars)

Pay it back on a schedule the trustees agree with you, in the open.
The block financing the block.
a down payment with no interest (1950s dollars)
high interest on a pawn, or the item gone (1950s dollars)
a fee on every check, for a year (1950s dollars)
more interest over a longer term (1950s dollars)

3% a month on a small loan, for a year (1950s dollars)

They'll hold your savings, but they won't lend a dollar on your street.
Your deposits fund mortgages across the line, year after year.
The red line on the federal map decides who gets to borrow.
savings that fund loans everywhere but your street (1950s dollars)
Furniture on time: a little each week.
The weekly price adds up to double the sticker or more.
Miss a week and they come for the whole set, paid-off pieces included.
The store makes more on the credit than on the furniture.
weekly furniture payments that double the price (1950s dollars)

You pay in for years; most policies like this lapse with nothing paid out.

Lapsed policies are the company's profit.
years of dimes on a policy that lapses (1950s dollars)
Borrow against your next paychecks: sign the wage assignment.
The lender takes your pay straight from your employer.
One late payment and your boss gets the notice, and may let you go.
Lenders and employers both profit from the hold it gives them over workers.
pay taken straight from your employer (1950s dollars)

Prices are marked up for credit customers, then interest goes on top.

credit markups plus interest (1950s dollars)

Lower payment, longer term: more interest, and the balloon is still at the end.
Signing resets the clock on everything you've paid in.
The seller gets paid again, and you still don't hold the deed.
more interest, and the balloon still at the end (1950s dollars)
Sell your next paycheck at a discount: cash today.
You hand over a full week's pay for most of it now. The discount is the interest.
Every payday it's due again, and it never stops.
Salary buyers worked the plant gates every payday.
a week's pay sold at a discount (1950s dollars)
Co-sign for your cousin's car. It's family.
You owe every dollar if they can't pay.
Their missed payment shows up on your name the same month.
Lenders count on family ties to collect.
every dollar of a car loan you cosigned (1950s dollars)

A fair rate. They lend where the downtown banks won't.
Clear terms, and you hold the deed from day one.
Owned by the community it lends to.
a fair mortgage on your own street (1950s dollars)

Member-owned: the profit comes back to the workers.
a small loan at a capped rate (1950s dollars)

Neighbors covering neighbors, the way the block always has.
a loan from the club, with no interest (1950s dollars)

interest charged on a year's store account (1870s dollars)

a crop pledged against a year of furnish (1870s dollars)

a balance carried over with interest into the next year (1870s dollars)

The merchant buys it for cash and sells it to you on time.
a season of fertilizer at the credit price (1870s dollars)

The man who weighs your cotton is the man you owe.
cotton weighed light and graded low at one settlement (1870s dollars)
A little cash for Christmas, against your share.
The advance is charged back to your share with interest added.
It comes out at next settlement, before anything else.
Small advances keep the account from ever coming out even.
a holiday advance repaid with interest (1870s dollars)

The mortgage covers the tools you need to farm at all.
One short year and he can take the mule and the plow.

a mule and tools held under a chattel mortgage (1870s dollars)

years of land payments lost with one missed year (1870s dollars)

The rent, the store bill and your share are all on one man's books.

a year's share settled on one man's books (1870s dollars)

savings paid for a land title that was worthless (1870s dollars)

a family's savings in a passbook (1870s dollars)

a year of sick and burial help from the society (1870s dollars)

a family's share of land bought together (1870s dollars)
Pay cash from the egg and garden money, at the cash price.
No credit price, no interest, and no lien on the crop.

Money the family made itself, kept off the merchant's books.
credit markups avoided on a season of goods (1870s dollars)

a family's half share after charges (1870s dollars)

a year of wages spent at one store's prices (1870s dollars)

fines and docked days over a season (1870s dollars)

a picking season weighed light (1870s dollars)

a year's share settled on figures you can't check (1870s dollars)

a year of farm wages held until settlement (1870s dollars)

a child's unpaid labor for a year (1870s dollars)

a share held back past the end of the year (1870s dollars)

lower terms with no one allowed to bid for your work (1870s dollars)

fare and fees taken out of a year's wages (1870s dollars)

a year of pay on terms someone else can check (1870s dollars)

better terms bargained for together (1870s dollars)

placement fees paid over and over for short jobs (1920s dollars)

lower pay for the hottest job, over a year (1920s dollars)

pay docked for 'breakage' over a year (1920s dollars)

days lost waiting at the gate, over a year (1920s dollars)

months laid off in a slow year (1920s dollars)

a year of marked-up prices at the company store (1920s dollars)

pay lost when a strikebreaker job ends with the strike (1920s dollars)

Free to look, with a small membership fee if you stay on.

Run by Black Dayton, for the people stepping off the train.
agent and placement fees you don't have to pay (1920s dollars)

Free: you just pass the word on to the next family that comes up.

Neighbors who already learned the hard way, looking out for you.
a bad agent's fee and a lost week avoided (1920s dollars)

a year of weekly board for a shared room (1920s dollars)

a year of rent marked up above what white tenants paid (1920s dollars)
